Macrons

Consonantal i

Theme

Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

worth adjective

worth doing, worth the trouble

also worth it, worthwhile, not worth it, worth seeing, worth the effort

classical

Ter. And. 217: audīreque eōrum est operae pretium audāciam
Plaut. Mil. 31b: nē hercle operae pretium quidemst
Traupman 409: it is worthwhile, operae pretium est; it isn’t worth it, nōn est operae pretium

operae pretium est

phrase, with an infinitive

it is worth while, worth the trouble

“The pay for the work”; operae pretium facere, to do something worth the effort (Liv. praef. 1).

Examples

  • Nē hercle operae pretium quidemst mihi tē narrāre tuās quī virtūtēs sciam.

    Really, it isn’t even worth your telling me of your exploits: I know them already.Plaut. Mil. 31b–32

  • ego paenitēre tantī nōn emō

    I don’t pay that much for something I’ll regretGell. 1.8.6

  • nihil dignum dictū āctum hīs cōnsulibus

    nothing worth telling happened in their yearLiv. 4.30.4

Other words

  • tantī est — it is worth it (the price, the trouble)

    phrase: genitive of value; nōn est tantī, it isn’t worth it · also used · classical · Cic. Cat. 1.22: sed est tantī, dum modo tua ista sit prīvāta calamitās; Gell. 1.8.6: ego paenitēre tantī nōn emō; Traupman 409: it’s not worth all that, tantī nōn est

  • dignus, digna, dignum — worth (telling, seeing), worthy of

    adjective, with the ablative, a supine in -ū, or quī and the subjunctive · also used · classical · Liv. 4.30.4: nihil dignum dictū āctum hīs cōnsulibus; Ter. Eun. 311: sīve adeō digna rēs est ubi tū nervōs intendās tuōs; Traupman 409: worthy (of), dignus (+ abl)

    With an infinitive only in verse and post-Augustan prose (Lewis & Short): Horātius ferē sōlus legī dignus, almost the only one worth reading (Quint. 10.1.96).

See also value.

SourcesLewis & Short: pretium (operae pretium) · Lewis & Short: tantus (tantī) · Lewis & Short: dignus

John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 409.
